question: \(\frac{2\sqrt6}{\sqrt2+\sqrt3+\sqrt5}\) equals
solution:
Group \(\sqrt2+\sqrt3\) as one quantity. Changing the sign of \(\sqrt5\) then creates a difference of squares, which removes that radical from the product:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(\sqrt2+\sqrt3+\sqrt5)(\sqrt2+\sqrt3-\sqrt5)\\
&\qquad=(\sqrt2+\sqrt3)^2-5\\
&\qquad=2+2\sqrt6+3-5=2\sqrt6.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(\sqrt2+\sqrt3+\sqrt5>0\), divide this identity by that quantity to obtain
\[
\frac{2\sqrt6}{\sqrt2+\sqrt3+\sqrt5}
=\sqrt2+\sqrt3-\sqrt5.
\]
The answer is choice A.
